## Every hop in your trace names its heuristic {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

**The case:** two victims paid a ransom to addresses R1 and R2. The agent asks where the money went. This afternoon's lab follows it to the first service, and every hop of that trace needs a reason a reader can check.

**Day 2 left off** with two clues to carry: co-spending and change. Today turns them into a method, in three parts:

1. **Link addresses into one actor:** co-spending, change, and how each fails.
2. **Follow the money forward and back:** peel chains, batches, backward traces and look-alike trails.
3. **Judge each hop:** a confidence for every row of the trace.

**By the end:** given a Bitcoin trace, write for each hop where the money went, the heuristic that says so, what could make it wrong, and how sure you are (High, Moderate or Low).

**The point to earn:** every hop rests on a heuristic that can fail: co-spending fails on a CoinJoin, and change rests on wallet habits. More clues from the same transaction stop at Moderate, so only a different kind of evidence makes a hop High [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013; @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide opens the day 6 tracing lesson with a case and a question: two victims paid a ransom, and the agent asks where the money went. It matters here because the afternoon's lab hands in an annotated trace, and every hop in it must name its heuristic, its failure and its confidence. Emphasize the objective: each part ends with a check, and the review asks the objective again.

**Key Points**
- Students already met both clues this lesson builds on. Day 2 (Reading a Transaction) taught them on "Co-spent inputs point to one owner" and "Change is the output back to the payer": two addresses spent together suggest one owner, and the leftover output suggests which is change. Today makes each a method and shows when it fails.
- The ransom case runs through the lesson. Part 1 links the ransom addresses, part 2 follows the money and meets a look-alike trail, and part 3 writes the trace rows. Its values are invented; the lab uses its own.
- Both heuristics come from Meiklejohn et al. (2013), and Kappos et al. (2022) describe co-spending as the one now widely used for tracing.
- The point is a claim the lesson earns, not one it assumes. Each heuristic can fail (co-spending on a CoinJoin, change whenever a wallet breaks its habits), and clues from one transaction are one kind of evidence. That is why they stop at Moderate.

New glossary terms this lesson: cluster, co-spend heuristic, change output, super-cluster, peel chain, peel, payment batching, backward trace, decoy trail.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the case and leave the agent's question open; the lesson answers it.
2. Read the link back to day 2, then name the three parts.
3. Read the objective aloud: by the end, every student can fill each row of a trace.
4. Time plan, 50 minutes: opening 3, part 1 12, part 2 15, part 3 12, close 8 (answers, review and next). The optional five-minute lab on the batching slide is outside the plan: run it only with time in hand.

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Co-spending links inputs, unless it's a CoinJoin {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** addresses spent together as inputs to one transaction most likely belong to one owner. That holds by habit, not by rule, and a CoinJoin breaks it on purpose.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **The heuristic:** all inputs to one transaction are controlled by the same user [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
- **Why it works:** each input needs its own key's signature, so multi-input transactions "necessarily reveal that their inputs were owned by the same owner" [@nakamoto_bitcoinpeertopeerelectronic_2008].
- **Why it fails:** a CoinJoin puts several people's inputs into one transaction [@gmaxwell_coinjoinbitcoinprivacy_2013]; spotting one is the work of Mixers and CoinJoin. A 2022 test set counts every cluster holding a CoinJoin as merging owners: 60 of its 120 [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].
- **How sure:** co-spending alone is **Moderate**.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 4.5
//| fig-height: 3.4
digraph CoSpend {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f8fafc", color="#cbd5e1", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=13];
  edge [color="#64748b", arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];

  A1 [label="A1", fillcolor="#fef3c7", color="#f59e0b"];
  A2 [label="A2", fillcolor="#fef3c7", color="#f59e0b"];
  T1 [label="Ordinary spend:\none wallet", fillcolor="#dcfce7", color="#22c55e"];
  X [label="Alice", fillcolor="#fef3c7", color="#f59e0b"];
  Y [label="Bob", fillcolor="#e0f2fe", color="#38bdf8"];
  Z [label="Carol", fillcolor="#fce7f3", color="#ec4899"];
  T2 [label="CoinJoin:\nthree owners", fillcolor="#fee2e2", color="#ef4444"];

  A1 -> T1; A2 -> T1;
  X -> T2; Y -> T2; Z -> T2;
  {rank=same; A1; A2; X; Y; Z;}
  {rank=same; T1; T2;}
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide teaches the co-spend (common-input-ownership) heuristic and its main failure. It matters here because co-spending is how a trace grows from one address to a cluster, and the lab asks for a confidence on every co-spend link. Emphasize that the heuristic rests on how wallets usually behave; a CoinJoin is built to defeat it.

**Key Points**
Start with the heuristic itself. Meiklejohn et al. state it this way: the inputs of one transaction are controlled by one user. Why should that hold? Each input needs its own key's signature, and Nakamoto's paper already named the leak: a transaction with several inputs reveals a common owner. But the heuristic holds because of how wallets usually behave, not because the protocol requires it, and a CoinJoin breaks it on purpose. A CoinJoin combines several users' inputs in one transaction, so applying co-spending to it merges strangers. In one test set that failure was common: Kappos et al.'s ground-truth set held 120 clusters, and the 60 false positives each contained one or more CoinJoins. That is why co-spending alone rates Moderate: one strong line, with a known false positive. The addresses co-spending links form a cluster, the set of addresses the analyst believes one entity controls, and the next slide shows how clusters grow.

**Walkthrough**
1. Left: A1 and A2 signed by one wallet. One owner, most likely.
2. Right: three people sign one transaction. The same shape, three owners.
3. Ask: from the inputs alone, can you always tell the two apart? (No; Mixers and CoinJoin shows the clues.)

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @nakamoto_bitcoinpeertopeerelectronic_2008
- @gmaxwell_coinjoinbitcoinprivacy_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## One false link merges two actors into one {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** a **cluster** is a set of addresses you believe one owner controls. Clusters grow by chaining: if A and B co-spend, and B and C co-spend, all three join. So one wrong link joins two whole clusters.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
- **Super-cluster:** false change links merged Mt. Gox, Instawallet, BitPay and Silk Road into one cluster of 1.6 million keys [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
- **A huge cluster is usually a service:** 20 ransomware addresses sat in clusters averaging 2.9 million addresses, all exchanges, wallets, mixers or markets [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].
- **So:** write down the heuristic behind every link, so a reader can find and cut a bad one.
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 4
//| fig-height: 3.8
digraph Merge {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f8fafc", color="#cbd5e1", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=13];
  edge [color="#64748b", arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11, dir=none];

  subgraph cluster_x {
    label="Actor X"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=12; color="#f59e0b"; style="rounded";
    A [label="A"]; B [label="B"]; C [label="C"];
  }
  subgraph cluster_y {
    label="Actor Y"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=12; color="#38bdf8"; style="rounded";
    D [label="D"]; E [label="E"];
  }
  A -> B [label="co-spend"];
  B -> C [label="co-spend"];
  D -> E [label="co-spend"];
  C -> D [label="one false\nchange link", color="#ef4444", fontcolor="#b91c1c", style=dashed];
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide shows why clustering errors are expensive: links are transitive, so one false link merges two entities. It matters here because the lab's trace and the attribution in Attribution and Confidence both depend on clusters a reader can audit. Emphasize recording the heuristic behind each link.

**Key Points**
The last slide ended on clusters; this one shows how a cluster goes wrong. Clustering chains links: if A and B co-spend, and B and C co-spend, all three join. So a single false link does not add one wrong address; it merges two whole clusters. Meiklejohn et al. warn that falsely linking even a few change addresses can collapse the graph into super-clusters, clusters that have wrongly merged many unrelated entities, and they hit one: a single super-cluster of 1.6 million public keys.

A huge cluster is not always an error, though. Kappos et al. found 20 of their ransomware addresses in clusters averaging 2.9 million addresses, all tagged as exchanges, hosted wallets, mixers or darknet markets, so that size suggests a custodial service, not one person. They add that nested services, services operating through accounts at an exchange, appear as the exchange under co-spending alone. So a huge cluster can be a real service or a super-cluster from false links, and that is why size alone stays Low, as the worked trace's step 4 shows. The habit that protects you is the slide's last line: write down the heuristic behind every link.

**Walkthrough**
1. A, B and C join by co-spending: actor X. D and E: actor Y.
2. One false change link from C to D.
3. Now X and Y look like one actor, and every conclusion about "them" mixes two people.

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Change is a guess from several weak clues {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .82em;"}

**Bottom line:** the change output returns money to the payer and moves the trace on. Every clue below is a wallet habit, so none is proof [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].

| Clue | Points to change when | Fails when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fresh address | Only this output's address is new [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013] | Both are new |
| Script type | Its type matches the inputs' [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022] | Payee's wallet is the same type |
| Un-round amount | 0.2937 beside a round 1.00 [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022] | Both are un-round |
| Output position | The wallet always puts change first, or last [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022] | The wallet varies it |
| Next hop alike | Later spent with the same transaction settings (version, locktime, SegWit) [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022] | Both are spent alike |
| Self-change | An output goes back to one of the inputs' own addresses [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013] | The wallet reuses addresses for payments too |
| Branches meet | Both outputs later reach one address and are spent together: co-spending says one holder got both [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013; @fbi_colonialaffidavit_2021, paras. 29-30] | That address is a service's |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20,52,28]"}

**How sure:** one clue alone is **Low**; several agreeing are **Moderate**, because all come from the same transaction. On a rough reuse test, 13% of Meiklejohn's first change labels looked wrong [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide turns day 2's change clues (Reading a Transaction) into a method: list the clues, say when each points to change and when it fails. It matters here because change detection decides where every hop of the trace goes next. Emphasize that agreeing clues raise confidence only to Moderate: they are one kind of evidence, the transaction's own shape.

**Key Points**
Co-spending grows a cluster; change moves the trace forward. A change output is the output that returns the unspent remainder of the inputs to the payer. Meiklejohn et al.'s change heuristic says a one-time change address is controlled by the inputs' owner, and they note it rests on an idiom of use, not on the protocol, so it is less robust than co-spending. That is why the table gives every clue a "fails when". Kappos et al. use address type, output index and the transaction features of the next hop, "the same transaction settings": version, SegWit, locktime and replaceability. They note that earlier change heuristics relied on address freshness and output values, including Ermilov et al.'s test that the change value is significant to at least the fourth decimal place.

Two rows need a word. Self-change is an output paid back to one of the inputs' own addresses: Meiklejohn et al.'s change heuristic leaves out transactions with one, and when you see one, that output is the change. Branches meet is not a new heuristic but co-spending applied later: if both outputs of one transaction land at one address and are spent together, one holder received both, so the split was not a payment to a stranger. It fails when that address belongs to a service holding many customers' coins. The Colonial Pipeline trace in Ransomware: the Payment and the Cash-out uses both clues, at hops 2 and 4.

How far can you trust the clues? Meiklejohn et al.'s first attempt flagged over 4 million change addresses. To estimate false positives they counted labeled addresses that were later reused: 13%. They judged many of those, such as Satoshi Dice payouts, not truly false, so the figure is rough, and refinements cut it, but the super-cluster on the last slide still formed. So on the course scale, amount or behavior alone is Low, and weaker lines that agree are Moderate. Independent means a different kind of evidence, so more clues from the same transaction, self-change included, do not make High.

**Walkthrough**
1. Take day 2's example: Alice pays Bob 1.00 and A3, new, gets 0.29.
2. Run down the table: fresh, same type, un-round. Three clues agree.
3. Rate it: Moderate. Ask: what would raise it to High? (A different kind of evidence, such as off-chain information; Attribution and Confidence.)

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @fbi_colonialaffidavit_2021
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Two outputs aren't always payment and change {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** when the clues don't tell the outputs apart, don't pick one. Write "change undetermined" and keep both as leads.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Two payees, no change:** mining pools and gambling sites often pay two people at once [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
- **Look-alike outputs:** in the Bitcoin Fog case (a Bitcoin mixer; part 2 returns to it), both outputs of one hop were fresh, of one type and spent alike; no change heuristic could follow it [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].
- **Wallets that break the habit:** some let the user choose or reuse the change address [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
- **What to do:** follow both outputs, or trace backward from where the money ended.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 4.5
//| fig-height: 3.6
digraph Undetermined {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f8fafc", color="#cbd5e1", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=13];
  edge [color="#64748b", arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];

  I [label="Input: 1.2441 BTC", fillcolor="#e1effa", color="#0072b2"];
  T [label="One transaction\nfee 0.0002 BTC", fillcolor="#f8fafc", color="#94a3b8"];
  O1 [label="0.5317 BTC\nfresh, bc1q"];
  O2 [label="0.7122 BTC\nfresh, bc1q"];
  Q [label="Which is change?\nUndetermined", shape=note, fillcolor="#fee2e2", color="#ef4444"];

  I -> T; T -> O1; T -> O2;
  {rank=same; O1; O2;}
  O1 -> Q [style=dashed, arrowhead=none];
  O2 -> Q [style=dashed, arrowhead=none];
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide teaches when change detection should stop: the two outputs look alike, or there is no change at all. It matters here because a forced change call is the false link two slides back. Emphasize that "undetermined" is a correct answer in the trace.

**Key Points**
The last slide gave the clues; this one says when to stop using them. First, not every two-output transaction has change: Meiklejohn et al. note that payments to two different users are frequent, such as mining pool payouts and bets on gambling sites. Second, even when there is change, the outputs can look alike. Kappos et al.'s Bitcoin Fog trace stalled going forward after one hop: both outputs had the same address features, were spent in transactions with the same features, and were both fresh. Third, some wallets break the habits the clues rely on: Meiklejohn et al. found that wallets letting users specify change addresses, and change addresses used twice, produced false change labels, and they excluded those cases. In each case a forced choice is the false link from two slides back. So record "change undetermined" and keep both outputs as candidates; that is better than a confident wrong hop.

**Walkthrough**
1. One input, two outputs, both fresh, both `bc1q`, neither round.
2. Run the table from the last slide: no clue separates them.
3. Write: change undetermined; candidates 0.5317 and 0.7122.

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Check: which output is change, and how sure? {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

The ransom has moved on. Transaction `T9` (invented) spends two addresses, K1 and K2, that the trace has reached:

```
Inputs   K1  bc1q...  0.8000 BTC
         K2  bc1q...  0.4500 BTC
Outputs  0   1Fh...   1.0000 BTC  seen before
         1   bc1q...  0.2496 BTC  first use      fee 0.0004 BTC
```

**Write two lines:** what links K1 and K2, and how sure? Which output is change, and how sure?

::: {.fragment}
**Answer:** K1 and K2 are co-spent, with no sign of a CoinJoin: one owner, **Moderate**. Output 1 is change: the only fresh address, the inputs' script type, and un-round beside a round 1.0000. Three clues from one transaction: **Moderate**, not High [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013; @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].

**Part 1 in one line:** co-spending links addresses by shared signing, change by wallet habit; write the heuristic behind every link, because one false link merges two actors.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide closes part 1 with a check every student answers: one invented transaction, two judgments. It matters here because the trace's first rows are exactly these two calls, and the common mistake is to rate three agreeing change clues High. Emphasize that both answers are Moderate, for different reasons.

**Key Points**
- The co-spend answer: K1 and K2 sign one transaction, so the co-spend heuristic links them to one owner. Two inputs and two unequal outputs show no sign of a CoinJoin, but CoinJoin remains the known failure, so it is Moderate.
- The change answer: output 1 is the only fresh address, it shares the inputs' bc1q script type, and its amount is un-round beside a round 1.0000. Three clues agree, but all come from this one transaction, so they are one kind of evidence: Moderate.
- The fee confirms the reading: 1.2500 in, 1.2496 out, so 0.0004 is the fee and no output is missing.
- The part's synthesis, on the slide: write the habit behind every link, because links chain and one false one merges two actors.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the transaction: inputs, then outputs.
2. Give every student a minute to write the two lines.
3. Ask for a show of hands: who wrote High for the change? Ask one of them why, then reveal the answer.
4. Read the part 1 synthesis.

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## A peel chain: a small peel, the rest rolls on {.smaller}

*Part 2: follow the money forward, then back.*

**Bottom line:** a peel chain starts with a large amount. Each hop pays a small amount (the **peel**) to one address and sends the rest to a fresh change address, which does it again, for hundreds or thousands of hops [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **Ordinary users and services make them:** exchange withdrawals and mining-pool payouts run as peel chains [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
- Services run scripts, so their chains are long and regular, which makes them easier to follow [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].
- **Thieves use them too:** stolen coins were gathered into one address, then peeled; some thieves peeled, re-gathered and peeled again [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 5.5
//| fig-height: 3.6
digraph Peel {
  rankdir=LR;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f8fafc", color="#cbd5e1", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=12];
  edge [color="#64748b", arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];

  S [label="Start\n20.000", fillcolor="#e1effa", color="#0072b2"];
  C1 [label="Change\n19.249", fillcolor="#fdf0d5", color="#e69f00"];
  C2 [label="Change\n18.048", fillcolor="#fdf0d5", color="#e69f00"];
  C3 [label="Change\n17.647", fillcolor="#fdf0d5", color="#e69f00"];
  M [label="...", shape=plaintext, style=""];
  P1 [label="Peel 0.750", fillcolor="#dff4ec", color="#009e73"];
  P2 [label="Peel 1.200", fillcolor="#dff4ec", color="#009e73"];
  P3 [label="Peel 0.400", fillcolor="#dff4ec", color="#009e73"];

  S -> C1 -> C2 -> C3 -> M;
  S -> P1; C1 -> P2; C2 -> P3;
  {rank=same; S; P1;}
  {rank=same; C1; P2;}
  {rank=same; C2; P3;}
}
```

Each hop also pays a 0.001 BTC fee.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
Part 2 follows the money forward, then back. This slide defines the peel chain, the most common pattern students will follow in the lab. It matters here because a peel chain is a run of change calls, so each hop inherits the change slide's clues and failures. Emphasize that peel chains are ordinary: services make them all day, so the pattern alone says nothing about crime.

**Key Points**
Now change at work over many hops. Meiklejohn et al. define the peeling chain: it starts with a large amount; at each hop a small amount, the peel, goes to one address and the remainder goes to a one-time change address, which does the same again, potentially for hundreds or thousands of hops. Leftovers may be gathered and peeled again. Why is the pattern so common? Kappos et al. explain that peel chains are fundamental to UTXO coins, because an output cannot be partly spent. So the pattern is ordinary: Meiklejohn et al. saw it in withdrawals from banks and exchanges and in mining-pool payouts, and Kappos et al. note that big services' scripted payments create long, patterned chains that are easier to follow. Thieves use the same shape: in Meiklejohn et al.'s theft cases, the Betcoin coins were gathered and then peeled, and the Bitfloor coins were peeled and gathered again and again. So the shape alone says nothing about crime. What it gives you is a run of change calls, each carrying the change slide's clues and failures.

**Walkthrough**
1. Start: 20.000 BTC.
2. Hop 1: 0.750 peeled; 0.001 fee; 19.249 rolls on as change.
3. Hop 2: 1.200 peeled; 18.048 rolls on. Hop 3: 0.400 peeled; 17.647 rolls on.
4. Ask: which output carries the chain forward? (The large change.)

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Follow the remainder; the peels are your leads {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** at each hop, the change output takes you to the next hop and the other output is the peel: the money's real recipient. Record every peel; the first one that lands at a service is where your trace ends [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].

- **Betcoin, 2012:** 3,171 BTC stolen in April 2012 sat unmoved until March 2013. It was then gathered into one address and peeled. After 10 hops a peel went to the Bitcoin-24 exchange; 10 hops later, one went to Mt. Gox. In all, 374.49 BTC reached known exchanges straight off the chain [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
- **Ransomware, 2022:** 96% of the peels from ransomware peel chains went to one-time addresses. That fits exchange deposit addresses, but the authors say it "does not clearly imply this" [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].
- **For each peel, record:** amount, address, hop number and what that address does next.
- **Naming the service** that owns a deposit address is attribution: Attribution and Confidence.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide teaches the tracing method for a peel chain: follow the change, collect the peels. It matters here because the lab's trace ends at the first service, and that is almost always a peel landing in a deposit address. Emphasize that a one-time recipient address suggests a service but does not prove it.

**Key Points**
The last slide showed the shape; this one shows how to follow it. Meiklejohn et al.'s method is to follow the change address to the next transaction at each hop; the other output, the peel, is the meaningful recipient. So the change is your path and the peels are your leads. Betcoin shows where that leads. It was hacked on 11 April 2012, and 3,171 BTC were stolen in four installments. The coins were gathered on 15 March 2013 and peeled. After 10 hops a peel went to the Bitcoin-24 exchange, and 10 hops later one went to Mt. Gox; in all, 374.49 BTC went to known exchanges directly off the main chain. Where do peels usually land? Kappos et al. collected 91,493 counterparty addresses from ransomware peel chains, and 96% were one-time addresses. That is consistent with exchange deposit addresses, but the authors stress it is not proof. So a peel at a one-time address suggests a service; linking that deposit address to a named service is attribution, taught in Attribution and Confidence.

**Walkthrough**
1. Return to the previous slide's chain: the green boxes are the path, the white boxes are the leads.
2. Tell the Betcoin story: wait, gather, peel, and peels reaching exchanges within 20 hops.
3. Ask: the 96% figure, is it evidence that the recipients are exchanges? (Weak and consistent, not proof: Low.)

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Batched payouts look busy but aren't a peel {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** services, "mainly exchanges", often pay many customers in one transaction, a **batch** [@bitcoinoptech_paymentbatching_2021]. A batch most often means a service paying out, so your trace has likely reached one: **Low** until attribution (Attribution and Confidence).

| | Peel-chain hop | Batched payout |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outputs | Two: one peel, one change [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013] | Many: one per customer, often plus change [@bitcoinoptech_paymentbatching_2021] |
| Inputs | The previous hop's change [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013] | The service's own, ideally just one [@bitcoinoptech_paymentbatching_2021] |
| What co-spending links | The inputs to the payer | The inputs to the service, never the customers to each other |
| What you write | Follow the change; record the peel | Likely a service (Low); your subject's output is the lead |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,36,42]"}

- **Why only Low:** any wallet can pay many outputs at once, and thieves split funds too [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013]; the shape alone is behavior.
- **Watch for:** exchanges also pay withdrawals as peel chains [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].

[Try it: Peel chain or payroll? (five-minute lab)](/assets/labs/peel-chain-or-payroll/index.html)

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide sets an exchange's batched payouts beside a peel chain. It matters here because a batch's many outputs can look like a suspect fanning money out, and misreading it sends the trace into dozens of unrelated customers. Emphasize the reading: a batch most often means the money is inside a service, and the output that matters is the one your subject received; but the shape alone is behavior, so it rates Low until attribution.

**Key Points**
A peel chain is one way money leaves a service; a batch is another, and it can look like a suspect fanning money out. Payment batching is paying many recipients in one transaction to save fees, and Bitcoin Optech says exchanges mainly use it. An unbatched payment typically has one input and two outputs, the receiver and change; a batch adds an output for each receiver, ideally from a single input. Optech lists reduced privacy as one cost: the recipients of one batch can assume a common sender.

Notice what a batch does not tell you. Co-spending links inputs only, so a batch says nothing about whether its recipients know each other. And Optech says services batch, not that only services do: any wallet can pay several outputs, and Meiklejohn et al.'s theft cases include thieves splitting funds. The shapes also overlap, since Meiklejohn et al. saw peel chains in exchange withdrawals too, so both can be a service paying customers. That is why a batch most often means a service, but the shape alone is behavior, and it stays Low until attribution.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the two columns row by row.
2. Ask: your subject's address is one of 40 outputs of a batch from an exchange. What do you write? (Funds likely came from a service, Low until attribution; if so, the subject withdrew from it and the other 39 are other customers.)
3. Optional, five minutes: open the Peel chain or payroll? lab from the link on the slide. Students predict which addresses belong in a suspect's cluster across a peel hop, a batched payout and a CoinJoin, put them in, meet the owner list, sort the three by shape, meet the term common-input-ownership heuristic, and see that a payment both sides add coins to looks normal.

**Sources**
- @bitcoinoptech_paymentbatching_2021
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013

:::

## When forward fails, trace backward {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** a trace can run either way. When change is undetermined going forward, start from where the money ended and work back. As described by Kappos et al. in 2022 [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022]:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **The question:** did a 2011 Mt. Gox withdrawal fund a deposit into the Bitcoin Fog mixer? Roman Sterlingov had a Mt. Gox account in his real name.
- **Forward:** every change heuristic stopped after one hop, at two look-alike outputs.
- **Backward:** from the deposit, the trace reached the withdrawal in seven hops.
- **Backward can mislead:** it gives more false positives than forward; in 2011 every transaction looked alike.
- **Record** the direction you traced and where forward stopped.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 4.5
//| fig-height: 3.8
digraph Backward {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f8fafc", color="#cbd5e1", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=13];
  edge [color="#64748b", arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];

  W [label="tx1: Mt. Gox withdrawal\n(he held an account there)", fillcolor="#fef3c7", color="#f59e0b"];
  H [label="tx2: two look-alike outputs\nforward stops", fillcolor="#fee2e2", color="#ef4444"];
  M [label="intermediate hops", shape=plaintext, style=""];
  D [label="tx3: Bitcoin Fog deposit", fillcolor="#e0f2fe", color="#38bdf8"];

  W -> H [label="forward"];
  W -> M [dir=back, label="backward:\n7 hops in all", color="#22c55e", fontcolor="#15803d"];
  M -> D [dir=back, color="#22c55e"];
  {rank=same; H; M;}
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide teaches the backward trace through a real case. It matters here because the lab's ransom trace may stall at an undetermined hop, and working back from a known endpoint is the way through. Emphasize the method, not the case's legal outcome, which is outside the course.

**Key Points**
Earlier, an undetermined hop stalled the trace. Here is the way through: a backward trace, following funds from where they ended to where they came from. Kappos et al. describe a real case in section 7.3.1. An IRS special agent's affidavit linked a 2011 deposit to the Bitcoin Fog cluster with a withdrawal from the Mt. Gox cluster, where Sterlingov had an account in his real name. The receiving and sending clusters were different, so co-spending alone could not link them; the affidavit said the withdrawal funded the deposit. Following forward failed after one hop: tx2's two outputs had the same address features, were spent in transactions with the same features, and were both fresh. Following backward from the deposit reached the withdrawal after seven hops, and the authors note the agent likely did this by hand.

Backward has its own risk. The authors warn it is more prone to false positives than forward: in 2011 all transactions had the same features, so a backward trace could run back indefinitely without noticing a change of owner. Here three deposit paths led to the same origin, which made them more sure. So when forward stalls, trace backward, and record which way you went.

Describe the case as the 2022 paper does; its later court history is not taught here.

**Walkthrough**
1. Top: the withdrawal. Forward, the trace stops at tx2.
2. Bottom: the deposit. Backward, hop by hop, the trace reaches tx1 in seven hops.
3. Ask: in your trace, which endpoints do you know? (The ransom address, and possibly a service's deposit.)

**Sources**
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Two trails, one service: walk each one back {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** a look-alike trail, a **decoy trail**, can end at the same service as yours. Walk each one back, and check the amounts. (Invented data: the ransom, 2.9140 BTC from R1 and R2, runs down a peel chain to deposit D.)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {style="font-size: .9em;"}
- **What you see:** the service spends deposits D and E together. E's trail has your thief's habits: round peels, `bc1q` change.
- **That sweep links D and E to the service,** not to each other's senders [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
- **Walk back:** E's trail reaches `Q0`, a coin with no path from R1 or R2.
- **Read the amounts:** `U1` spent 4.0000 BTC, more than the whole ransom (2.9140); outputs never exceed inputs, so the ransom alone could not have funded it [@bitcoin.orgdevelopers_transactionsdeveloperguide_2024]. The walk back shows none of it came from R1 or R2.
- **Write:** E is a separate trail; the ransom reached the service at D.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 4.6
//| fig-height: 4.0
digraph Decoy {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f8fafc", color="#cbd5e1", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=12];
  edge [color="#64748b", arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];

  R [label="R1 + R2\nransom 2.9140", fillcolor="#fef3c7", color="#f59e0b"];
  T [label="Peel chain"];
  D [label="Deposit D", fillcolor="#dcfce7", color="#22c55e"];
  Q [label="Q0: no path\nfrom R1 or R2", fillcolor="#fee2e2", color="#ef4444"];
  U [label="U1 ... U3\ninput 4.0000", fillcolor="#fee2e2", color="#ef4444"];
  E [label="Deposit E"];
  S [label="Service sweep:\nD and E spent together", fillcolor="#e0f2fe", color="#38bdf8"];

  R -> T -> D -> S;
  Q -> U -> E -> S;
  {rank=same; R; Q;}
  {rank=same; D; E;}
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide teaches how to tell a look-alike trail from the real one when both end at the same service. It matters here because the afternoon's trace includes a trail like this, and following the wrong one hands the agent the wrong deposit. Emphasize the two tests: walk each trail back, and read the amounts.

**Key Points**
The backward trace on the last slide has a second use. Suppose the ransom's peel chain ends in deposit D, and the service later spends D in one transaction with another deposit, E. E's trail looks like yours: round peels, the same address type, the same pace. Is E the ransom too? The sweep cannot say. Co-spending links D and E to whoever held their keys at the sweep, the service, and says nothing about who sent to them. So walk E's trail back, hop by hop, the way the Bitcoin Fog trace went. It reaches Q0, a coin with no path from R1 or R2. Then read the amounts. Every Bitcoin transaction's outputs add up to no more than its inputs, and the difference is the fee, so value cannot appear from nowhere. E's trail once held 4.0000 BTC in a single input, more than the whole ransom of 2.9140, so the ransom alone could not have funded it. The amounts cannot rule out part of the ransom mixed with other money; the walk back to Q0 does, because none of E's coins came from R1 or R2. Matching habits are behavior, the weakest evidence on the scale; a trail's origin and its amounts are what decide. So write E down as a separate trail, and keep D as the ransom's arrival. The values are invented; the lab's trail has its own.

**Walkthrough**
1. Left of the diagram: the ransom trail, R1 and R2 down a peel chain to deposit D.
2. Right: E's trail, from Q0 through U1 to U3 to deposit E. Point out the habits it shares.
3. Bottom: the sweep spends D and E together. Ask: does that make E ransom money? (No: it links both deposits to the service.)
4. Walk E back to Q0, then compare 4.0000 with 2.9140. Ask: which test would you trust if only one were available? (The walk back decides; the amounts confirm it. Record both.)

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @bitcoin.orgdevelopers_transactionsdeveloperguide_2024

:::

## Check: peel chain, batch or decoy? {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

Name each pattern, and say what you follow next.

1. One input pays 0.3000 BTC to one address and 6.8412 BTC to a fresh one, which does the same again, and again.
2. One input pays 45 different addresses, plus one output back to the payer.
3. A second trail with your thief's habits reaches the same service as yours, but walks back to a coin that never touched the ransom.

::: {.fragment}
**Answers:** 1 is a **peel chain**: follow the 6.8412 change and record the 0.3000 peel as a lead. 2 is a **batch**, most often a service paying out: Low until attribution; only your subject's output is the lead [@bitcoinoptech_paymentbatching_2021]. 3 is a **decoy trail**: its origin never touched the ransom, so record it as separate. Reaching the same service links it to the service, not to your thief [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].

**Part 2 in one line:** follow the change and collect the peels; when forward stalls or trails look alike, walk back and read the amounts.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide closes part 2 with a check: three short patterns, each named and given its next step. It matters here because the lab's trace meets all three, and naming the shape decides where the trace goes next. Emphasize that each answer ends in an action: follow, stop, or set aside.

**Key Points**
- Pattern 1 is a peel chain, Meiklejohn et al.'s shape: a small peel to one address and a large remainder to a fresh change address, repeated. The change is the path; the peel is a lead.
- Pattern 2 is a batch, which Bitcoin Optech says exchanges mainly use. It most often means a service paying out, so it is Low until attribution, and the customers in it are not linked to each other.
- Pattern 3 is the decoy trail from the last slide: it shares the habits but not the origin, so it is set aside, not merged into the ransom trace.
- The part's synthesis, on the slide: follow the change, collect the peels, and when forward stalls or two trails look alike, walk back and read the amounts.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the three patterns.
2. Give students a minute to name each one and write what they follow next.
3. Take answers for each in turn, then reveal.
4. Read the part 2 synthesis.

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @bitcoinoptech_paymentbatching_2021

:::

## Same-transaction clues never reach High alone {.smaller}

*Part 3: write each hop with its confidence.*

::: {style="font-size: .9em;"}

**Bottom line:** confidence rises with independent evidence, not more clues: clues from the same transactions stop at Moderate.

| Hop rests on | Confidence | Why, on the course scale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Change from one clue, such as a round amount | **Low** | Amount or behavior alone |
| Co-spending, no sign of a CoinJoin | **Moderate** | One strong line; CoinJoin is a known false positive |
| Several change clues that agree | **Moderate** | Weaker lines, all from the same transaction |
| A long peel chain with a steady pattern | **Moderate** | One kind of evidence: the pattern |
| Any of these, plus another kind of evidence (Attribution and Confidence) | **High** | Independent lines agree; no known failure applies |

: {tbl-colwidths="[42,16,42]"}

Investigators "should not rely on" these heuristics "as definitive evidence": a careful actor defeats them [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
Part 3 turns each hop into a written row with its confidence. This slide applies the course confidence scale to the heuristics taught so far. It matters here because every hop in the lab trace carries a confidence, and the common mistake is to count clues instead of kinds of evidence. Emphasize the definition: independent means a different kind of evidence, not a second heuristic over the same transactions.

**Key Points**
Most slides so far gave a confidence; this one puts them all on one scale. Low is timing, amount or behavior alone, or one unverified label. Moderate is one strong line, or weaker lines that agree, with a known false positive possible. High needs two or more independent lines that agree, with no known failure applying, and on-chain heuristics alone do not get there. Why not? Kappos et al. warn that randomizing transaction and address features defeats their heuristics, and that investigators should not rely on them as definitive evidence. They add that all clustering heuristics share these limits but still work, because many entities do not evade them. So use the heuristics, and give every hop a word from this scale, never a percentage.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read each row and its reason.
2. Ask: three change clues agree; is that High? (No: Moderate. Same transaction, same kind of evidence.)

**Sources**
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## From one raw transaction to two trace rows {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** a trace row is built from what the explorer shows. Read the inputs, then the outputs, and write one row per judgment. (Invented data: the next slide's `T1`.)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
```
Transaction T1         fee 0.0003 BTC
Inputs
  R1  bc1q...  1.5000 BTC  (ransom)
  R2  bc1q...  1.4140 BTC  (ransom)
Outputs
  0   3J7...   0.5000 BTC  seen before
  1   bc1q...  2.4137 BTC  first use
```
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
1. **Inputs:** R1 and R2 are spent together, so one wallet signed both: **co-spend**. Is `T1` a CoinJoin? Two inputs, two unequal outputs, no other owners' coins: no sign of one. Row 1: **Moderate**.
2. **Outputs:** run the change clues. Output 1 is the only fresh address, the same `bc1q` type as the inputs, and un-round beside a round 0.5000.
3. **Three clues agree:** change is output 1, so call it C1. All three come from this one transaction. Row 2: **Moderate**.
4. **Next:** follow C1; output 0 (P) is a lead.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide shows the steps that turn raw explorer output into the first two rows of the worked trace on the next slide. It matters here because the lab asks students to make these rows themselves, and the finished table alone hides how each row was reached. Emphasize the order: inputs first (co-spend), then outputs (change), then one row per judgment.

**Key Points**
Now the heuristics on one real-looking transaction. The data are invented, and they match steps 1 and 2 of the next slide. Read the inputs first. Two ransom addresses are spent together in one transaction, so Meiklejohn et al.'s co-spend heuristic links them to one owner. A CoinJoin would break that, but nothing here looks like one: two inputs, and two outputs of unequal amounts. So the first row is Moderate. Then read the outputs. Three change clues from the change slide agree: output 1 is the only fresh address, it has the same script type as the inputs, and it is un-round beside a round amount. Those clues come from Kappos et al., who use script type and value features, and Meiklejohn et al., who use freshness. Check the fee as you go: the inputs minus the outputs, 2.9140 minus 2.9137, is 0.0003 BTC, which confirms you have read every output. Several clues from one transaction are still one kind of evidence, so the second row is Moderate too.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the raw view top to bottom: inputs, then outputs.
2. Walk steps 1 to 4 on the right; at step 2, point at each clue in the raw view.
3. Ask: if output 0 had also been a first use, what changes? (The fresh-address clue drops out; script type and amount still point to output 1, so the call stands at Moderate. If the remaining clues disagreed, you would write "change undetermined".)

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## A worked trace: four steps, four judgments {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .9em;"}

**Bottom line:** your lab product looks like this: one row per judgment, with its heuristic, its failure and its confidence. (Invented data.)

| Step | What you see | Heuristic | Could be wrong if | Confidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Ransom R1 and R2 spent together in `T1` | Co-spend: one wallet | `T1` is a CoinJoin | Moderate |
| 2 | `T1` pays 0.5000 to P, 2.4137 to C1 | Change is C1: fresh, same type, un-round | C1 is the payment | Moderate |
| 3 | C1 peels 0.1 to 0.6 over hops `T2` to `T6` | Peel chain: follow the change | A peel was the change | Moderate |
| 4 | `T6`'s peel to D; D's cluster: 2 million addresses | Huge cluster: likely a service | It is not a service | Low |

: {tbl-colwidths="[7,30,26,22,15]"}

Stop at step 4: the money has reached what looks like a service. Naming it, and raising that Low, is attribution (Attribution and Confidence).

**Ask:** which row would you check first if the conclusion were challenged?

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide models the annotated trace the lab asks for, on invented data; the previous slide built its first two rows from the raw transaction. It matters here because students see a finished product before they build one. Emphasize that every row names a heuristic and a failure, and that the trace stops at the first service.

**Key Points**
The last slide built two rows. This is the whole trace, again on invented data; the lab uses its own captured data. A row is one judgment, so one transaction can give two rows, as steps 1 and 2 do, and a whole peel chain can give one, as step 3 does. Step 1 is co-spending of two ransom addresses in one transaction: Moderate, because a CoinJoin would break it. Step 2 reads the same transaction's outputs: three change clues agree, and that is Moderate, since they are one kind of evidence. Step 3 follows a peel chain of five transactions by its change, so each hop inherits the change heuristic's failure. Step 4 is where the trace stops. The last peel lands in address D, later co-spent into a cluster of about 2 million addresses. That is service-sized, like the 2.9 million average on the false-link slide, and a huge cluster is usually a service, but size alone is behavior, so it is Low until attribution.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read each row left to right: what moved, why you think so, what would make you wrong, how sure.
2. Ask: why does the trace stop at step 4? (It has reached the first service.)
3. Ask: which row would you check first if the conclusion were challenged? (The weakest: step 4.)

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Practice: write the trace rows for three hops {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

For each hop, write one row per judgment: the heuristic, what could make it wrong, and how sure you are (High, Moderate or Low). All three are invented.

```
A  Inputs   W1 bc1q 0.6000, W2 bc1q 0.9000
   Outputs  0  3Ka... 0.5000 seen before   1  bc1q... 0.9995 first use
B  Input    bc1q 1.2000
   Outputs  0  bc1q... 0.7000 first use    1  bc1q... 0.4997 first use
C  Input    bc1q 1.0000
   Outputs  0  bc1q... 0.4251 first use    1  bc1q... 0.5745 first use
   (both later spent in transactions with the same settings)
```

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
The three parts are done; this slide has students write the trace rows the lab asks for, on three hops that need three different judgments. It matters here because the afternoon's trace is built from rows like these, and each hop tests a different part of the lesson. Emphasize that "undetermined" is a valid row.

**Key Points**
- Hop A tests part 1's two heuristics together: a co-spend, then a change call with three clues.
- Hop B has two fresh bc1q outputs, so only one clue, the un-round amount, separates them.
- Hop C has outputs that look alike in every way the lesson taught, the Bitcoin Fog problem from part 1.
- The answers, with their reasons, are on the next slide; keep it hidden until students have written theirs.

**Walkthrough**
1. Give students five minutes in pairs to write the rows for each hop: one per judgment.
2. Remind them to check each fee: inputs minus outputs.
3. Take answers for hop A before moving on, then B, then C.

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Answers: three hops, three judgments {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .8em;"}

| Hop | Heuristic | Could be wrong if | Confidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | Co-spend: W1 and W2 have one owner. Change is output 1: fresh, the inputs' type, un-round beside 0.5000 [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013; @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022] | A is a CoinJoin; output 1 is the payment | **Moderate** for each row |
| **B** | Change is output 1: un-round beside a round 0.7000 [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022] | The payee asked for an un-round amount | **Low:** one clue |
| **C** | None separates the outputs: change undetermined [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022] | Not applicable: no call is made | **None given:** no change call is made; keep both as leads and trace back from where the money ends |

: {tbl-colwidths="[8,46,26,20]"}

Fees: A 0.0005, B 0.0003, C 0.0004. Each one confirms every output was read [@bitcoin.orgdevelopers_transactionsdeveloperguide_2024].

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide gives the answers to the practice, each with its heuristic, its failure and its confidence. It matters here because the feedback is where students check their own rows against the habit the lab grades. Emphasize the reasons: Moderate for hop A, because three clues from one transaction are one kind of evidence; Low for hop B, because one clue is behavior alone.

**Key Points**
- Hop A is two rows, like steps 1 and 2 of the worked trace. The co-spend of W1 and W2 is Moderate, because a CoinJoin is its known false positive. The change call is Moderate too: the fresh address is Meiklejohn et al.'s clue, and the script type and amount are Kappos et al.'s.
- Hop B rests on one clue. Both outputs are fresh and of one type, so only the un-round 0.4997 points to change, and one clue alone is Low.
- Hop C is the Bitcoin Fog problem: both outputs are fresh, of one type and spent alike, so no change heuristic can follow it. The right row says "change undetermined" and keeps both outputs as leads; a backward trace from where the money ends is the way through.
- The fees: inputs minus outputs gives 0.0005, 0.0003 and 0.0004. A fee that comes out negative or far too large means an output was misread.

**Walkthrough**
1. Reveal the slide after students have written their rows.
2. Read each row; ask a pair who chose a different word to say why.
3. Ask: what would raise hop A to High? (A different kind of evidence, such as an exchange's records; Attribution and Confidence covers it.)

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022
- @bitcoin.orgdevelopers_transactionsdeveloperguide_2024

:::

## Review: every hop, a heuristic and a confidence {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .8em;"}

**The objective:** given a Bitcoin trace, write for each hop where the money went, the heuristic that says so, what could make it wrong, and how sure you are. Answer each question from memory before the answer appears.

**1. R1 and R2 are spent together. What does that suggest, what breaks it, and how sure?**

::: {.fragment}
One owner; a CoinJoin breaks it; **Moderate** [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013; @gmaxwell_coinjoinbitcoinprivacy_2013].
:::

**2. Three change clues agree. Is that High?**

::: {.fragment}
No, **Moderate**: all three come from one transaction. Only a different kind of evidence raises it [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].
:::

**3. No clue separates the two outputs. What do you write?**

::: {.fragment}
"Change undetermined"; keep both as leads, and trace back from where the money ends [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].
:::

**4. A trail like yours reaches the same service. How do you tell it from the ransom?**

::: {.fragment}
Walk it back to its first coin, and check the amounts: outputs never exceed inputs [@bitcoin.orgdevelopers_transactionsdeveloperguide_2024].
:::

**5. Where does the trace stop, and why is that hop only Low?**

::: {.fragment}
At the first service. A huge cluster is usually a service, but it could be a super-cluster made by a false link [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013; @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].
:::

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide reviews the lesson against its objective: five questions, answered from memory before each answer appears. It matters here because recalling an answer fixes it better than hearing a summary, and the questions show whether students can now write every row of a trace. Emphasize question 2: rating agreeing clues High is the mistake the lesson most wants to stop, asked a second time.

**Key Points**

- Question 2 is the part 1 check asked again, and the lesson's point: clues from one transaction stop at Moderate.
- Question 3 is part 1's last slide: undetermined is a correct row, and the backward trace from part 2 is the way through.
- Question 4 is part 2's decoy trail: the origin and the amounts decide, not the habits.
- Question 5 is part 3's worked trace: the trace stops at the first service, and size alone is behavior.

## Recall: UTXO vs. Account Model {.smaller}

| | **Bitcoin (UTXO)** | **Ethereum (Account)** |
|---|---|---|
| **How value moves** | Outputs are created and consumed — each coin has a traceable history | Balances update in place — accounts persist and change state |
| **Tracing unit** | Individual UTXOs (discrete coin fragments) | Addresses and contract interactions |
| **Where evidence lives** | Transaction inputs and outputs | Transaction record + event logs + internal call traces |
| **Hidden value flows** | Rare — the tx record is mostly complete | Common — ERC-20 transfers and internal calls are invisible without parsing logs |
| **Primary heuristic** | Common-Input-Ownership (CIOH) | Contract interaction clustering |

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This opening comparison slide establishes that Bitcoin and Ethereum require different forensic mental models because value and evidence are recorded differently. It matters here because the rest of the lesson depends on not applying UTXO heuristics blindly to account-based systems. Emphasize that the tracing unit changes the entire investigative workflow.

**Key Points**
- Bitcoin traces discrete outputs, while Ethereum often traces persistent accounts, contract calls, and event logs.
- Analysts need to know where evidence actually lives before selecting heuristics or tools.
- Spell out UTXO as unspent transaction output and define event log as contract-emitted data that records token and application activity.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @salisu_blockchainforensicsmodern_2023

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Reminder: Bitcoin's UTXO Model

Transactions **consume** old outputs and **create** new ones. Every satoshi has a traceable ancestry.

::: {style="z-index: -1; position: relative; top: -75px; max-height: 440px; overflow: hidden;"}

```{dot}
//| echo: false
//| fig-height: 2.2
digraph UTXO {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f5f7fb", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=8];

  utxo_a [label="UTXO A\n0.6 BTC", fillcolor="#e1effa", color="#0072b2"];
  utxo_b [label="UTXO B\n0.5 BTC", fillcolor="#e1effa", color="#0072b2"];
  tx [label="Transaction", shape=ellipse, fillcolor="#f8fafc", color="#94a3b8"];
  out1 [label="Output 1\n1.0 BTC\n(Payee)", fillcolor="#dff4ec", color="#009e73"];
  out2 [label="Output 2\n0.09 BTC\n(Change)", fillcolor="#fdf0d5", color="#e69f00"];

  utxo_a -> tx;
  utxo_b -> tx;
  tx -> out1;
  tx -> out2;
}
```

:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Implication:** If you know one input address, the Common-Input-Ownership Heuristic (CIOH) lets you cluster all co-spent inputs as the same owner. Outputs can be identified as payment vs. change using heuristics.
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes the UTXO model as the foundation for classic Bitcoin forensics heuristics. It matters here because later heuristics such as CIOH and change detection only make sense in this model. Emphasize that value moves by consuming and recreating outputs rather than mutating balances in place.

**Key Points**
- Every Bitcoin transaction consumes prior outputs and creates new ones with their own traceable histories.
- The structure makes payment and change inference possible when paired with heuristics.
- Define CIOH briefly as the common-input-ownership heuristic that assumes co-spent inputs are controlled by one entity.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @salisu_blockchainforensicsmodern_2023

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Reminder: Ethereum's Account Model

Accounts **persist**. Transactions update balances — and trigger contract code, which may move value through many more contracts in a single block.

::: {style="z-index: -1; position: relative; top: -50px; max-height: 400px; overflow: hidden;"}

```{dot}
//| echo: false
//| fig-height: 2.2
digraph Ethereum {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10, fillcolor="#f5f7fb"];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];

  eoa [label="EOA\n(Your Wallet)", fillcolor="#E6F7FF"];
  contract [label="Smart Contract\n(e.g., Uniswap)", fillcolor="#fff5cc"];
  token [label="Token Contract\n(e.g., USDT)", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
  eoa2 [label="EOA\n(Recipient)", fillcolor="#E6F7FF"];

  eoa -> contract [label="1. Call swap()"];
  contract -> token [label="2. Internal call"];
  token -> eoa2 [label="3. Transfer event (log)", style=dashed, color="#2ecc71", fontcolor="#2ecc71"];
}
```

:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Implication:** The top-level transaction may show $0 ETH transferred. All value movement is in the logs. You must parse every contract's event log to follow the money.
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes the account model as the reason Ethereum forensics often requires deeper parsing than Bitcoin. It matters here because a simple transaction view can hide most of the actual value movement. Emphasize that contracts, logs, and traces must be read together.

**Key Points**
- Ethereum accounts persist over time, and contracts can trigger many downstream actions from one top-level transaction.
- Analysts often need logs and traces because top-level ETH value fields can be misleading or zero.
- Define internal trace briefly as the record of contract-to-contract execution steps inside one transaction.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @salisu_blockchainforensicsmodern_2023

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## The Analyst's Mindset: Graph Thinking {.smaller}

Blockchain forensics is fundamentally **graph analysis**. On-chain data is represented as a network of nodes and edges to uncover patterns of activity.

-   **Nodes:** Addresses, UTXOs, or **entity clusters** — a real-world actor assumed to control all addresses in the cluster.
-   **Edges:** Transactions or value flows between nodes.

::: {style="position: relative; top: -140px; overflow: hidden; max-height: 410px; z-index: -1; padding: 0; margin: 0;"}

```{dot}
//| echo: false
//| fig-height: 2.2
digraph GraphThinking {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f5f7fb", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];

  addr_a [label="Address A"];
  addr_b [label="Address B"];
  entity1 [label="Entity 1\n(Cluster: A+B)", shape=ellipse, fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
  addr_c [label="Address C"];
  entity2 [label="Entity 2\n(Cluster: C)", shape=ellipse, fillcolor="#ffdddd"];

  addr_a -> entity1 [style=dashed, label="belongs to"];
  addr_b -> entity1 [style=dashed];
  addr_c -> entity2 [style=dashed, label="belongs to"];
  entity1 -> entity2 [label="Transaction", penwidth=2];
}
```


:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" style="position:relative; top:-100px;"}
By identifying recurring **motifs** — fan-outs, fan-ins, peeling chains — analysts can infer entity behavior and intent.
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes graph thinking as the core analytical mindset for blockchain forensics. It matters here because the lesson is about patterns of movement and control, not isolated transactions. Emphasize that the analyst's job is to collapse many addresses and flows into interpretable entity behavior.

**Key Points**
- Nodes can represent addresses, outputs, or clustered entities, and edges represent value movement or relationships.
- Recognizable graph motifs help analysts infer laundering strategies, service roles, or operational intent.
- Define entity cluster briefly as a set of addresses inferred to be controlled by one real-world actor or service.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @frowis_safeguardingevidentialvalue_2020

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Graph Motif: The "Fan-Out"

A **Fan-Out** occurs when a single source sends to many destinations.

```{dot}
//| echo: false
//| fig-height: 1.8
digraph FanOut {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f5f7fb", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];
  input [label="Input", fillcolor="#e3f2fd", color="#0d6efd", fontcolor="#0d6efd"];
  source [label="Single Source", shape=ellipse, fillcolor="#ffdddd"];
  dest1 [label="Dest 1"];
  dest2 [label="Dest 2"];
  dest3 [label="Dest 3"];
  dest_n [label="...", style=dotted];

  input -> source;
  source -> dest1;
  source -> dest2;
  source -> dest3;
  source -> dest_n;
}
```

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes the fan-out as a basic graph motif whose meaning depends heavily on context. It matters here because many benign and malicious behaviors can look similar at first glance. Emphasize that pattern recognition must always be paired with domain interpretation.

**Key Points**
- A fan-out means one source distributes value to many destinations.
- Exchanges, payouts, dusting attacks, and laundering steps can all produce fan-out shapes.
- Define dusting briefly as sending tiny amounts to many addresses to tag or study them.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @frowis_safeguardingevidentialvalue_2020

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Graph Motif: The "Fan-In"

A **Fan-In** consolidates many inputs into a single destination.

```{dot}
//| echo: false
//| fig-height: 1.8
digraph FanIn {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f5f7fb", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];
  source1 [label="Source 1"];
  source2 [label="Source 2"];
  source_n [label="...", style=dotted];
  dest [label="Single Destination", shape=ellipse, fillcolor="#ffdddd"];
  output [label="Output", fillcolor="#e3f2fd", color="#0d6efd", fontcolor="#0d6efd"];

  source1 -> dest;
  source2 -> dest;
  source_n -> dest;
  dest -> output;
}
```

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes the fan-in as the opposite graph motif: many sources consolidating into one destination. It matters here because consolidation often signals service infrastructure, laundering preparation, or fund aggregation. Emphasize that destination context determines whether the fan-in is routine or suspicious.

**Key Points**
- Fan-in patterns often appear when deposits are being aggregated before further movement or cash-out.
- A known destination label can turn a generic fan-in into a strong investigative lead.
- Define consolidation briefly as gathering funds from many addresses into a smaller number of controlled destinations.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @frowis_safeguardingevidentialvalue_2020

:::
